newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair offers to ease ban on Sinn Fein contact.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair offers to ease ban on Sinn Fein contact.

text.p: Britain's new Prime Minister Tony Blair on Friday offered to ease a ban on official contacts with the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, to help find a negotiated settlement to the Northern Ireland conflict.

He said in a speech that he would allow his government officials to meet Sinn Fein provided the Irish Republican Army did not carry out further acts of violence in its 28-year-old campaign to end British rule in Northern Ireland.
"I am prepared to allow officials to meet Sinn Fein provided events on the ground, here and elsewhere, do not make that impossible," he said at a Belfast farming fair.
The governments of Britain and Ireland have banned contacts with Sinn Fein since the IRA resumed its war by ending a 17-month ceasefire in February 1996.
Blair said only an unequivocal IRA ceasefire would allow Sinn Fein to take part in Belfast peace talks which resume on June 3.

But his offer to allow his officials to meet Sinn Fein was the first new initiative on Northern Ireland since the IRA began bombing Britain and Northern Ireland again to press for an unconditional place at the Belfast talks.
Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams and Martin McGuinness have been calling on Britain to reopen contact with Sinn Fein since they were both elected to the British parliament in the May 1 election.

Both men, who have refused to occupy their seats because it would entail an oath of allegiance to the British rule they want to end, say they should be at the Belfast talks by virtue of their electoral mandate.

Blair, making Northern Ireland his first visit outside London since he won election, sought to reassure Protestant Unionists who want the province to remain British that he would not be making sweeping concessions to Catholic Irish nationalists who want it reunited with Ireland.

"My agenda is not a united Ireland, and I wonder just how many see it as a realistic possibility in the foreseeable future. Northern Ireland will remain part of the United Kingdom as long as the majority here wish," he declared.
But Blair acknowledged that Northern Ireland was "fragile and fraught" and said a settlement between Unionists and Nationalists should be achievable if peace prevailed.
"Violence has no place in a democratic society, whatever the motivation of those practicing it," said Blair, on the day that a Roman Catholic killed in cold blood by Protestant loyalists was buried.
Sean Brown, 62, was shot dead by suspected Loyalists extremists this week, the third person to die in 10 days of violence by pro-and anti-British extremists.
David Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionist Party, the province's biggest pro-British grouping, played down the implications of Blair's comments.

"My understanding...is that it is from the point of view of making sure they (Sinn Fein) understand the government's position rather than entering in any form of talks or negotiations," he told BBC television.
"I don't see anywhere in this speech any weakening of the position with regard to a ceasefire or entry into talks."
